5.9 State Emergency Response Teams

RIEMA, in conjunction with local jurisdictions, maintains a variety of emergency response teams who can rapidly identify, evaluate, and react to a wide spectrum of emergencies and provide support via the Emergency Management Assistance Compact. The following is a brief summary of these teams:

Rhode Island Heavy Rescue Task Force

This Task Force is organized into the East Bay (Middletown, Newport, and Portsmouth Fire Departments) and West Bay (Warwick Fire Department) Heavy Rescue Squad. When the two squads come together, they form the Rhode Island Heavy Rescue Task Force that is a Type-4 Urban Search and Rescue asset.

Hazardous Materials and Mass Decontamination Team

This Team is made up of six Hazardous Material Teams (Cranston, East Providence, Hope Valley, Providence, Warwick, and Woonsocket), and four Decontamination Teams (Hopkins Hill, Kingston, North Kingstown, and North Providence). The teams are used to assess and manage the consequences of a hazardous materials/WMD release, either accidental or as part of a terrorist attack.

Rhode Island Critical Stress Management Team

This Team is made up of six Hazardous Material Teams (Cranston, East Providence, Hope Valley, Providence, Warwick, and Woonsocket), and four Decontamination Teams (Hopkins Hill, Kingston, North Kingstown, and North Providence). The teams are used to assess and manage the consequences of a hazardous materials/WMD release, either accidental or as part of a terrorist attack.

Rhode Island Critical Stress Management Team

This team is designed to be a comprehensive, multi-component, multi-discipline program providing stress and crisis management to any fire, police, or ambulance department personnel responding to a critical incident, multi-casualty event, or disaster.

Rhode Island Disaster Medical Assistance Team

This Team recruits and trains medical health professionals to respond to public health emergencies and is currently comprised of over 800 volunteers.

Rhode Island Medical Reserve Corps

The Medical Reserve Corps has over 1,200 registered health volunteers who are called upon to assist in public health and emergency situations.

Wilderness Search and Rescue Team

This Team formalizes search and rescue capabilities and enhances efforts with the utilization of civilian volunteers. While the operations of all missing person searches shall remain a law enforcement function, there is a need to integrate the services of both trained and untrained civilian volunteers into a large-scale search effort.

Weapons of Mass Destruction Tactical Team

This Team is made up of members from the Rhode Island State Police and is used to contain, control, and de-escalate hostile situations where the use of weapons of mass destruction has been, or threatened to be, introduced.

Flammable Liquids Task Force

This Team is made up of members from the Rhode Island State Police and is used to contain, control, and de-escalate hostile situations where the use of weapons of mass destruction has been, or threatened to be, introduced.

Flammable Liquids Task Force

This Task Force (East Providence, Johnston, Providence, Warwick, Valley Falls, and Woonsocket Fire Departments) protects life, property, and critical infrastructure by using its assets to contain, control, and extinguish fires, or releases and spills involving flammable or combustible liquids or gasses. The Task Force uses five Williams Foam Trailers with 660 gallons of Aqueous Film Forming Foam-Alcohol Resistant Thunderstorm Foam Concentrate in 330-gallon totes to extinguish liquid and gaseous fires.

Port of Providence Marine Strike Team

This Team (Providence, East Providence, Cranston, and Warwick) is a waterside asset to mitigate chemical, incendiary, environmental and life safety incidents that occur in the port of Providence or contiguous waters. Each team has one boat, with the capability to conduct nighttime Search and Rescue, fire suppression, hazmat detection, weapons of mass destruction detection, and can support emergency medical services and dive operations.

5.11 Local Jurisdiction Capabilities Assessment

5.11 Local Jurisdiction Capabilities Assessment

Currently, all State of Rhode Island jurisdictions have an emergency management program that has the primary responsibility for local response, recovery, hazard mitigation planning. During a local or state disaster, the head of the local government and/or the director of the local emergency management program can activate their local emergency operation center and establish direct communications with both RIEMA and State political leadership. However, the capability of each emergency management program varies based largely on the size and financial capabilities of the jurisdiction. While all jurisdictions have the capability needed to conduct mitigation planning, many rely on the technical expertise of RIEMA to apply for grant funding and oversee mitigation projects. Augmenting local emergency management capabilities, RIEMA aids with state and federal mitigation and emergency management initiatives and available funding opportunities. Other local personnel capabilities vary widely, and again are often tied to jurisdiction size and financial capabilities. In general, more urban, or larger jurisdictions have a greater range of full-time personnel dedicated to planning, engineering, mapping, and response, while smaller jurisdictions lack these capabilities.

[Context: 5.11 Local Jurisdiction Capabilities Assessment]

Technical capabilities for each jurisdiction vary widely and are generally based on financial capabilities. As with personnel, and in general, more urban, or larger jurisdictions have a greater range of technical capabilities related to planning, engineering, mapping, and response, while smaller jurisdictions lack these capabilities. It should be noted that RIEMA offers a variety of programs to provide local jurisdictions with technical expertise, including mapping and planning.

A review of local level hazard mitigation plans indicates that most local jurisdictions have limited funding sources for mitigation initiatives and rely on available state or federal grant programs. However, tax generated funding (often generated from property and/or sales tax) can be allocated to infrastructure improvements for schools, public works, and other government functions. In addition, some larger jurisdictions have dedicated transportation or capital improvements sales or use taxes that can be obligated to fund mitigation projects.

On a yearly basis, many jurisdictions throughout the State of Rhode Island fully allocated their tax revenue to basic services and programs. As a result, funding for mitigation projects is often unavailable or severely limited. While the capability to assess special taxes or issue bonds does exist, historically it has been shown that passing these measures is extremely difficult. As a result, many needed mitigation projects throughout the state are not completed due to lack of funding. It should be noted that RIEMA offers a variety of programs to provide local jurisdictions with financial expertise, including grant application and determining potential funding streams.

6.4 Barriers to Local Hazard Mitigation Planning

RIEMA recognizes that creating local Hazard Mitigation Plans can present a burden to local jurisdictions. Potential barriers that have been identified include:

[Context: 6.4 Barriers to Local Hazard Mitigation Planning]

• Resource Constraints: Limited financial, personnel, and time resources can be a significant barrier. High turnover in staffing is also a concern that we see in Rhode Island. The state sees many of the same planners, but they seem to switch around within communities, so the lack of continuity is a concern. Also, the inconsistency of who is the responsible party for updating the local hazard mitigation plan varies in communities. Many communities think it belongs to the Emergency Management Agency Directors, which often means it falls on a part-time employee who doesn’t have the adequate time to dedicate to an update and often misses an opportunity to apply for funding, resulting in an expired plan. • Political Leadership: A lack of political leadership can hinder the development and adoption of mitigation plans or a lack of understanding the importance of a hazard mitigation plan. • Competing Priorities: Communities often face various challenges and priorities, which can divert attention and resources away from hazard mitigation planning. Most communities in Rhode Island are understaffed and taking on job responsibilities that are out of their job scopes. • Short-Term Focus: Communities may prioritize immediate needs over long-term planning. Many communities in Rhode Island are not preparing for the renewal of their hazard mitigation plan and the expiration date comes as a surprise and applying for funding is time consuming. • Institutional Barriers: Bureaucratic barriers, lack of inter-agency coordination, or inefficiencies can hinder the mitigation planning process. • Funding and Grants: While funding can be a resource constraint, communities may also struggle to secure grants and financial support for mitigation projects, especially if they lack the expertise or

[Context: 6.4 Barriers to Local Hazard Mitigation Planning]

capacity to navigate the complex grant application process. The FEMA application and grant award process is extremely time- consuming. Applications for a plan update can take between four months to 11 months to be approved, which in turn delays securing a consultant and then plans expire in the meantime. FEMA contributes to these delays due to a lack of staff, which mirrors staffing challenges the state and local municipalities are facing. Unfortunately, these delays greatly impact the municipalities desire to apply for funding, which we have seen causes plans to expire. • Technical Expertise: A lack of in-house expertise can be a barrier, especially for smaller communities. Many small communities do not have a town planner and their Emergency Management director is responsible for applying for a grant to update the plan while having several lifesaving community responsibilities.

Overcoming these barriers requires a concerted effort, commitment, and support from local, state, and federal agencies, as well as the community.

[Context: 6.4 Barriers to Local Hazard Mitigation Planning]

To help overcome these barriers, RIEMA continues to provide as much technical assistance to local planners as time and staffing allows. In addition, and in order to standardize in-state planning efforts and minimize planning variances, RIEMA has worked to develop a local hazard mitigation template for local planners. This template will provide both a recommended structure and recommended content which are matched to FEMA’s local guidance. RIEMA, specifically the State Hazard Mitigation Officer, is tracking dates and reaching out to communities three years before their plan expires to explain the importance of applying for funds early. RIEMA is also helping communities by standardizing the components of an application for a plan update as much as possible, allowing use components as necessary. Recently RIEMA has asked to join the Governor’s monthly municipal call to let the highest governing authority in the communities and the Governor know about funding opportunities and the importance of having an updated plan. RIEMA has also visited two municipalities that appeared on local news after flooding events to discuss BRIC and project scoping, and how it can help, providing they have an updated plan. RIEMA will continue to do presentations to inform local jurisdictions of available funding opportunities to those who have a current hazard mitigation plan. Lastly, RIEMA has adopted Element H (from the review tool), which requires local municipalities to provide a month when they are going to hold their annual Hazard Mitigation Plan meeting. RIEMA will be tracking these months and reaching out around the time they designated to follow up on their annual meeting.

6.5 Review and Approval of Local Hazard Mitigation Plans

When a plan is submitted to RIEMA for review it is logged and assigned to a reviewer. Any subsequent information regarding the plan is then tracked until the plan reaches final FEMA approval. The plans are reviewed in the order in which they are received. When possible, RIEMA will review plans within 30 days of their submission. If revisions are necessary, the period for resubmittal will vary depending on the request for information. RIEMA will then submit the plan to FEMA Region I where it should be reviewed within 45 days whenever possible.

If revisions are needed, FEMA will notify RIEMA and RIEMA will notify the jurisdiction within five business days. Depending on the request for information will determine how long the jurisdiction takes to resubmit to RIEMA. Once the revised plan is submitted to RIEMA, it will be logged and reviewed in the order that it was received and resubmitted to FEMA Region I.

If the plan is deemed acceptable, FEMA will notify the local municipality directly with a copy to RIEMA that the plan has reached approved pending adoption status or fully approved if adopted before submission. The jurisdiction then must obtain resolutions from the participating jurisdictions. Once final resolutions are received, the local municipality will then submit the final mitigation plan to FEMA Region I. FEMA then issues a final approval letter.

In general, federal and state funding for mitigation planning and projects is limited and often competitive. When reviewing initial requests for assistance with mitigation planning and projects, RIEMA considers:

• As a principal consideration, does this project maximize potential benefits • Availability of funds • A demonstrated desire and capability to complete the planning process • The jurisdiction has the ability to complete proposed mitigation projects • Expiration date of current plan, if applicable When funding because available RIEMA advertises a notice of intent period. Notice of intents are received for a limited amount of time then graded on various criteria to determine which ones will be selected to develop planning applications. • Is this project for a mitigation plan development or update?

Available federal funds for pre-disaster and post-disaster mitigation grants will most likely not be sufficient to support all eligible project applications. None the less, an attempt will be made to award grants to the maximum number of eligible projects. When considering hazard mitigation projects, the State of Rhode Island attempts to align priorities with that of FEMA. As such, RIEMA uses the priorities outlined in the FEMA Notice of Funding Opportunity to prioritize project applications. When funding comes from the HMGP, priority is given to mitigation projects which are related to the hazard that necessitated the disaster declaration and those jurisdictions included in the disaster declaration. In the event that there are not enough eligible projects to use these criteria, RIEMA places a priority on local mitigation projects that:

[Context: 2024 State of Rhode Island Hazard Mitigation Plan Page 312]

• Involve non-structural and lower cost solutions such as updating and enforcing local flood ordinances, retrofitting high-risk structures, or the acquisition of repetitive loss structures. • Exhibit: cost-effectiveness as established by a benefit cost ratio calculated using the FEMA Benefit-Cost Analysis software. • Contribute the greater solutions to stated problems. • Are in communities with the highest risk. • Address repetitive flood loss. • Are proposed by communities with the most intense development pressure. In evaluating hazard mitigation applications for grant funding, a scoring system is used to prioritize projects according to both federal eligibility criteria and the State eligibility criteria as published in the grant application guidance. For each round of grant funding, RIEMA reviews the applications. Mitigation projects submitted for consideration for grant funding are evaluated using a scoring process emphasizing protection of life and property, reduction of risk, and cost- effectiveness. Proposed mitigation projects must also comply with the goals and objectives in both the local hazard mitigation plan and the SHMP. Additionally, for mitigation projects seeking federal funding, applicants must follow national priorities and requirements as detailed in the specific grant program guidance literature. RIEMA staff work with each grant applicant to ensure that proposed projects meet these criteria. When prioritizing grant applications, the seriousness of risk is emphasized when considering an applicant's response to the following federal and State eligibility criteria. Among the criteria receiving greatest weight in scoring are those dealing with reduction of risk posed by hazards, prevention of repetitive loss structures, and protection of critical areas

[Context: 2024 State of Rhode Island Hazard Mitigation Plan Page 312]

including frequently flooded areas and geologically hazardous areas.

Project Eligibility

All projects seeking to receive either pre- or post-disaster grant funding must meet the following criteria as determined by RIEMA:

• Must be in conformance with a FEMA-approved local and/or multi-jurisdictional all hazards mitigation plan which meets the mitigation planning requirements per the Disaster Mitigation Act of 2000. • Must be in conformance with the Rhode Island SHMP. • Must be in, or have a beneficial impact upon, past declared disaster areas or in a high-risk area for potential impacts a natural hazards. The high-risk area should be identified in either the local, regional, or State mitigation plan. • Must be in compliance with all existing Rhode Island Laws and Regulations for construction, land alterations, and natural resource protection. • Must be in compliance with municipal ordinances and zoning regulations. • Must be in conformance with 44 CFR, Part 9, Floodplain Management and Protection of Wetlands, and 44 CFR, Part 10, Environmental Considerations. • Must provide a solution to a problem independently or provide a significant functional portion of a solution being addressed in a combined project. 6.8 Utilization of Local Plan Data in 2024 SHMP

RIEMA provided all available local mitigation plans for data integration purposes into the SHMP. A comprehensive review was conducted of all currently approved local hazard mitigation plans to integrate the local risk assessments into the state’s analysis. Collected data was then translated into a unified model that accounted for any variability in methodologies. The result of this assessment provides a larger scale snapshot of how local jurisdictions view risk and allows both local and state planners to integrate data into plans with a whole picture methodology. By integrating data across plans the overall planning efforts of the State become more robust. Additionally, all mitigation strategies were reviewed and incorporated into the revision of state strategies to ensure statewide unity of effort.

For this SHMP, each of the above referenced local hazard mitigation plans was reviewed for the following elements, with data incorporated into the state plan:

7.2 Mitigation Problem Statements

As part of this planning process, the SIHMC worked to identify gaps and deficiencies both in State and local capabilities and hazard assessment. Resulting from this assessment is a series of problem statements, concise descriptions of issues or challenges that needs to be addressed:

[Context: 7.2 Mitigation Problem Statements]

• Local Hazard Mitigation Plans contain inconsistent data that is difficult to combine on a State level. • Continued climate change is driving an increased incidence of major hazard occurrences, stressing the response, recovery, and mitigation capabilities of even the most prepared jurisdiction. • Understanding and utilization of climate change models and predictions is underutilized in local plans. • The expansion of hazard areas related to sea level rise and storm surge inundation will continue to increase the number of State and local facilities and assets at risk. • The aging dam infrastructure and lack of analysis on vulnerability is compounded by staffing challenges, potentially decreasing inspections and data output. • With the potential advent of greater periods of drought, and the large footprint of WUI areas in the State, Rhode Island is at increased risk for a large and destructive wildfire event. • Despite attempts to engage all communities to ensure planning equity, little buy-in was achieved. • The hardening of aging state assets against identified hazards will be costly and slow. • The difficulties in applying for and managing hazard mitigation grants are beyond the capability of smaller jurisdictions. • Engagement with the public on hazard mitigation, and actions they can take to protect themselves and their property, are lacking. • Staffing at all levels is stretched thin, with many personnel wearing multiple hats, compromising planning, response, recovery, and mitigation capabilities. To overcome these identified challenges, RIEMA, the SIHMC, and participating stakeholders will work collaboratively using the following strategies as appropriate:

The RI READY program is a statewide industrial site readiness initiative designed to prepare sites to achieve pre- permitted status. This program provides access to an array of services designed to create an inventory of pre-permitted properties ready for industrial development throughout the State. State investment is recaptured to the extent possible to make the initiative self-sustaining and extend the life of available funds. The RI READY program leverages the Quonset Development Corporation, a quasi-state agency which partners with both Rhode Island Commerce and municipalities and/or private parties to spur development activity throughout the state. Site-readiness awards are made in two categories, site-specific improvements, and municipal assistance. Site-specific improvements include site planning and pre-development activities and project improvements. Projects intended to catalyze growth in advanced industry clusters, regardless of project size, are prioritized. Municipal Assistance awards are for developing projects that will lead to further growth and support the municipality’s development goals.

Federal Programs

FEMA provides financial assistance to state, local, tribal, and territorial governments, as well as certain private non- profit organizations, to implement projects that help reduce the risk and impact of future disasters. These grant programs are designed to support initiatives aimed at mitigating hazards and improving resilience. The main grant program offered by FEMA for hazard mitigation is the Hazard Mitigation Assistance (HMA) program. The HMA program includes four subprograms, the Hazard Mitigation Grant Program (HMGP), the HMGP Post-Fire, Building Resilient Infrastructure and Communities (BRIC), and the Flood Mitigation Assistance (FMA) grant program. Applicants to these grant programs are required to submit project proposals that demonstrate the effectiveness of their proposed mitigation projects. The eligibility criteria, application process, and specific requirements for each program are outlined by FEMA in their guidelines and announcements, which are typically published on FEMA’s website.

Section 8 – Plan Maintenance

8.1 Introduction

The SHMP is a living document that will be updated and submitted to FEMA for approval every five years as required by 44 CRF 201.4. During the five-year cycle, the plan will undergo continuous monitoring and evaluation to ensure that the policies, procedures, priorities, and state environment established in the plan reflect current conditions. RIEMA has developed a method to ensure monitoring, evaluation, and updating of this SHMP. RIEMA will utilize the SIHMC to provide plan updates, revisions, and data collection for future HMP planning purposes.

8.2 Plan Update Responsibilities

RIEMA serves as the lead coordinating agency for emergency management in Rhode Island, including plan maintenance. Additional participants in the plan maintenance process include members of the SIHMC, subject matter experts, and representatives of local jurisdictions.

The SIHMC will facilitate the review and revision of the SHMP every five years. The review and revision will be an ongoing process. This process will incorporate all of the revisions made during the annual plan review, especially new data obtained from the local hazard mitigation plans. As these plans are completed, new information relative to hazards and threats will be incorporated into the formal five-year update.

8.3 Plan Review Meetings

The SIHMC will meet bi-annually for the first two years after plan approval. If needed, more meetings will take place during this timeframe. The RIEMA SHMO will determine the meeting dates and location and is responsible for sending invitations. RIEMA will be the main point of contact for these meetings and will maintain attendance and meeting minutes.

The purpose of these meetings is to discuss agency capability changes, the status of proposed projects, and any new studies or mapping that may inform the SHMP. Should a specific plan element or section require revision or amendment prior to the subsequent plan revision due to state or federal legislation or policy change, RIEMA staff will meet with all appropriate stakeholders and propose the change or addendum to FEMA as quickly as is practicable.

A robust participation from these stakeholders for the dam safety program adds greater value to the risk assessment.  As listed in the State Mitigation Planning Policy Guide (2022), potential actions to reduce vulnerabilities to/from high hazard potential dams include: o Proposing, enacting, and/or delegating authority for local land use regulations, ordinances, and/or other standards to protect life and property from high hazard potential dams. o Working with dam owners to create/update and share EAPs or dam incident annexes to emergency operations plans. o Delegating authority to local governments to adopt and enforce land use ordinances in inundation zones. o Acquiring structures both upstream and downstream of high hazard potential dams. o Rehabilitating and/or removing high hazard potential dams.
